intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 109818337: a cook who talks to plants, painting clouds, out of curiosity. Here is how that became a hut on a hill, a runner bean called Houston, and a lot of silver paint.

rolls.value: a cook who talks to plants
rolls.became: The cook at the hut on the hill. They talk to everything that grows, and most of all to the runner bean by the door, which they call Houston and talk to the way astronauts talk to Houston. So every log line is radio chatter, and the cook's call sign is Kitchen.
Every cloud has a silver lining, they say. The cook checked: not one cloud over the hut has one. So the cook paints them on with a pastry brush on a long bamboo pole, from a basket hauled up Houston.

Four layers of them, from fat cumulus over the hut up to tiny cirrocumulus ripples, each further up and each holding more rain. And above them all, the Big One, which has sat over the hill since before the hut was built.

Why paint a lining just to scratch it off? Because a cook knows what a lining is for: line a tin, and whatever's inside comes out clean. A lined cloud is a scratch card. Scratch through it and the inside releases, clean: rain, mostly.

What's behind each lining is decided when it's painted: a few litres of rain, or hail (five times the rain, and a dent in the hut roof that stays), or now and then something the sky lost. A kite, a glove, a paper plane, a party balloon, a weathervane cockerel, a small warm meteorite. Each one moves into the garden and does something there.
Litres of rain and metres of bean. Houston grows from a cane by the door to 600 m, and nothing costs more than about nine hundred litres.
The cook just wants to know what's inside a cloud. The first answer is rain. So is the second. The cook keeps asking anyway, higher each time.

Clouds are high, so the cook needs Houston to grow (watered with the rain, which is tidy). And the missions are physics turned up for a minute: a crosswind that blows clouds past at three times the speed, warm air that thins them to nothing in six seconds, and a moonless dark where you see only by head-torch.

rolls.value: challenges: replay under a handicap for a reward
rolls.became: Those three missions. Each replays a minute of sky under one law of physics, and winning it earns something for good: a windsock (more clouds come by), pan lids for the rain-butts (no rain evaporates), and the head-torch (you can see hail glinting through a lining).
Houston, the runner bean. Named by the cook, for obvious radio reasons.

Houston grows tendrils and starts scratching clouds herself, unprompted, logged as initiative. She listens to the shipping forecast on the radio and wears the chef's hat. And at the very end she's the one who goes up.

rolls.value: an ending reached by holding back
rolls.became: At 600 m the Big One rolls in, and the cook lines all of it, glinting with hail. The final mission is not to scratch it, because scratching rains it out. The countdown only runs while nobody scratches, so the cook comes down, puts their hands in their apron pockets, and Houston climbs in alone. At the top she says her first words: “Kitchen, this is Houston. We have a view.”
About half an hour: four cloud layers, three missions, thirty cans of water for Houston, and one very long minute at the end.

The hilltop is a little slab of turf and soil, like a model on a shelf: the hut, the bean bed, the pumpkins and the bamboo, all in isometric, with the clouds drifting over it at four heights and an altimeter down the side.
Night purples and navy for the sky, mauve and tan for moonlit cloud, mint and cream for the silver linings, deep teal and blue for the rain inside, scarlet for the bean flowers.

Slow, wide pads in D phrygian under a few glassy bells, like telemetry from very far up. A soft pulse joins for missions, and for the hold it goes almost still. The sound effects use the same scale, so scratching plays a little climbing tune as the lining comes off.
Kitchen to Houston, release confirmed, logged as initiative. Houston only ever answers with a rustle. Until she doesn't.

The game is set on the night it was released: 21 November 2026, a waxing gibbous moon, 87% lit and three nights from the full Beaver Moon. It's drawn exactly that shape in the corner, and the cook keeps mentioning it.

outro: In short: an idiom made the linings, a cake tin made the scratch card, the rain made the bean grow, and the bean made the ending. Kitchen, out.
